title: CT SB00004: An Act Concerning Consumer Privacy And Protection.

obligations: A data broker must not sell or license brokered personal data in this state on or after January 1, 2027, unless actively registered with the Department of Consumer Protection (Sec. 2(a))
A data broker that intends to sell or license brokered personal data must submit an application for initial registration with a $2,500 fee, and renew annually with a $2,500 fee (Sec. 2(b))

Each registration application must disclose the applicant's name, contact information, primary Internet web site, a publicly accessible web page detailing consumer rights without dark patterns, whether it collects minors' personal data or precise geolocation or reproductive or sexual health data, measures to ensure no unlawful sale, regulatory status, and other required information (Sec. 2(c))

Each registered data broker must establish a privacy policy that includes measures to ensure it does not sell or license personal data in violation of sections 1 to 10 or sections 42-515 to 42-526 (Sec. 3)

The Commissioner of Consumer Protection must establish and periodically update an Internet web page disclosing registered data broker information and providing access to the accessible deletion mechanism (Sec. 4)

The Commissioner must establish an accessible deletion mechanism program by July 1, 2028, with specified features including consumer submission of deletion requests, status checks, updates, broker exclusion, disability accessibility, security safeguards, and consumer explanations (Sec. 5(a)(1))
The Commissioner must use a consumer's motor vehicle operator's license number solely to verify deletion requests and updates, and must not share, store or retain it (Sec. 5(a)(2)(A))
Each deletion request and update is confidential and not a public record under the Freedom of Information Act (Sec. 5(a)(2)(B))

On and after August 15, 2028, the Commissioner or authorized agent must verify deletion requests using the operator's license number and update the mechanism, or specify that unverified requests be processed as an opt-out under section 42-518(a)(5)(B) (Sec. 5(b))

On and after October 1, 2028, each registered data broker must access the accessible deletion mechanism at least once every forty-five days to examine deletion requests and updates, and for each verified request not excluding the broker, delete personal data and direct data service providers to delete, or for unverified requests, retain and process as an opt-out (Sec. 5(c)(1))

A registered data broker must repeat the deletion actions at least once every forty-five days after first deleting a participating consumer's personal data, unless the consumer submits a verified update specifically excluding the broker (Sec. 5(c)(2))
The Commissioner may impose a fee on each registered data broker that accesses the accessible deletion mechanism, not exceeding the cost of providing access (Sec. 5(c)(3))

On and after October 1, 2028, a registered data broker or data service provider that deletes a participating consumer's personal data must not maintain, use or disclose any personal data subsequently acquired concerning that consumer (Sec. 5(c)(4))
A registered data broker that retains personal data under an exception must not maintain, use or disclose it for any other purpose (Sec. 5(c)(5)(B))

By July 1, 2031 and triennially thereafter, each registered data broker must retain an independent auditor to audit compliance with subsection (c) of section 5, prepare an audit report, and maintain the report and materials for at least six years (Sec. 5(d)(1))

A registered data broker must submit an audit report and materials to the Department of Consumer Protection within five business days after the department sends notice requiring submission (Sec. 5(d)(2))

By July 1, 2029 and annually thereafter, each business that was a registered data broker during the preceding calendar year must post a statement on its primary Internet web site disclosing the total number of deletion requests accessed, how many were responded to by deleting, retaining, or both, and the number retained based on exceptions or exemptions (Sec. 6)

A person doing business in the state who uses a price setting device for any reason other than to establish a discounted price in an online transaction and advertises or promotes online a price established by the device must include the disclosure 'THIS PRICE WAS INCREASED BY A PRICE SETTING DEVICE USING YOUR PERSONAL DATA' or a substantially similar disclosure, readily visible to the average consumer (Sec. 11(b))

A retail seller or third-party delivery service that offers a discounted price under the exception in section 11(c)(2)(C) must prominently post the discounted price and uniform terms and conditions on its Internet web site in readily understandable language and offer the discounted price to all consumers pursuant to those terms (Sec. 11(c)(2)(C)(I),(II))

A controller must limit collection of personal data to what is reasonably necessary and proportionate, not process for new purposes without consent, establish reasonable data security practices, not process sensitive data without consent, not process personal data in violation of discrimination laws, provide an effective consent revocation mechanism, not sell sensitive data without consent, and not process personal data for targeted advertising or sell personal data of known minors aged 13 to 17 (Sec. 14(a)(1))
A controller must not discriminate against a consumer for exercising consumer rights (Sec. 14(a)(1) last sentence)

A processor must adhere to the instructions of a controller and assist the controller in meeting obligations, including responding to consumer requests, security, breach notification, and data protection assessments (Sec. 15(a)(1))

A controller or consumer health data controller that uses facial recognition technology on its premises for security purposes must exclusively use it to match still images or video to a database maintained exclusively by the controller, and post clearly legible signage at each entrance alerting consumers and including a conspicuous hyperlink or quick response code to the facial recognition technology policy (Sec. 16(a)(2)(A))
A direct-to-consumer genetic testing company must transact its business consistent with a consumer's rights under section 18 (Sec. 19(a)(1))

A direct-to-consumer genetic testing company must disclose its policies and procedures concerning collection, use and disclosure of genetic data prior to accepting any biological sample, genetic data or payment (Sec. 19(a)(2))

A direct-to-consumer genetic testing company must display a prominent and publicly accessible privacy notice on its Internet web site disclosing policies and procedures concerning collection, use, access, disclosure, transfer, security, retention and deletion of consumer data and consent (Sec. 19(a)(3))

A direct-to-consumer genetic testing company must obtain express consent before collecting, using or disclosing a consumer's genetic data, after disclosing policies, identity of persons who may access results, and manner of disclosure (Sec. 19(a)(4))

A direct-to-consumer genetic testing company must separately obtain express consent to disclose or transfer genetic data to any person other than a vendor or service provider, to use genetic data for any purpose other than the primary purpose, or to retain a biological sample after completion of testing (Sec. 19(a)(5))

A direct-to-consumer genetic testing company must obtain informed consent in accordance with 45 CFR 46 for any disclosure or transfer of genetic data to a third party for research purposes or research conducted under the company's control for publication or generalizable knowledge (Sec. 19(a)(6))

A direct-to-consumer genetic testing company must implement reasonable security measures to protect biological samples and genetic data from unauthorized access, destruction, use, modification or disclosure (Sec. 19(a)(9))

A direct-to-consumer genetic testing company must implement a process for a consumer to access genetic data, require deletion of genetic data, require destruction and confirmation of destruction of biological sample, and revoke consent for research use by the company or third parties (Sec. 19(a)(10))
prohibitions: No data broker shall sell or license brokered personal data in this state on or after January 1, 2027, unless actively registered with the Department of Consumer Protection (Sec. 2(a))
No data broker shall sell or license any personal data in violation of sections 1 to 10 or sections 42-515 to 42-526 (Sec. 3)

No registered data broker or data service provider that deletes a participating consumer's personal data shall maintain, use or disclose any personal data subsequently acquired concerning that consumer (Sec. 5(c)(4))

No registered data broker or data service provider that maintains, uses or discloses a participating consumer's personal data for an exception shall maintain, use or disclose it for any other purpose (Sec. 5(c)(5)(B))

No person doing business in the state who uses a price setting device for a non-discounted online price shall advertise, promote, label, or publish online a price without including the required disclosure (Sec. 11(b)(1))
No retail seller or third-party delivery service doing business in the state shall engage in surveillance pricing (Sec. 11(c)(1))
No controller shall sell any consumer's precise geolocation data (Sec. 14(a)(3)(A))
No third party shall sell any consumer's precise geolocation data (Sec. 15(a)(2)(A))
No controller shall process personal data in violation of any state or federal law that prohibits unlawful discrimination against consumers (Sec. 14(a)(1)(E),(F))

No controller shall process sensitive data concerning a consumer without obtaining the consumer's consent, or in the case of a known child, without processing in accordance with COPPA (Sec. 14(a)(1)(D))
No controller shall sell the sensitive data of a consumer without the consumer's consent (Sec. 14(a)(1)(H))

No controller shall process personal data for targeted advertising or sell personal data of a consumer under circumstances where the controller has actual knowledge or wilfully disregards that the consumer is at least 13 but younger than 18 years of age (Sec. 14(a)(1)(I))
No controller shall discriminate against a consumer for exercising consumer rights (Sec. 14(a)(1) last sentence)

No direct-to-consumer genetic testing company shall disclose the results of any genetic testing to any person other than the consumer, unless the company has obtained express consent or the disclosure is made pursuant to a court order, warrant or subpoena (Sec. 19(a)(7))

No direct-to-consumer genetic testing company shall disclose a consumer's genetic data to the consumer's employer, to any person offering health, life or long-term care insurance or providing information to insurers for underwriting, or to any third party the company knows or reasonably should know intends to use the data for marketing including targeted advertising (Sec. 19(a)(8))

No streaming video service shall transmit to a consumer the audio of a commercial advertisement at a volume louder than the volume of the video content that accompanies the commercial advertisement, on and after July 1, 2027 (Sec. 20(b))

No controller or consumer health data controller using facial recognition technology on premises for security shall use it other than exclusively to match still images or video to a database maintained exclusively by the controller (Sec. 16(a)(2)(A)(i))
reading.what_it_does: This act requires data brokers selling or licensing brokered personal data in Connecticut to register with the Department of Consumer Protection and participate in a statewide accessible deletion mechanism for consumer deletion requests. It also prohibits certain surveillance pricing and requires disclosure when a price setting device increases a price using personal data, imposes consent and control obligations on direct-to-consumer genetic testing companies, and limits commercial advertisement volume on streaming video services.
reading.effective_date: October 1, 2026 (general effective date; specific compliance dates: January 1, 2027 for data broker registration, July 1, 2028 for accessible deletion mechanism establishment, August 15, 2028 for verification, October 1, 2028 for broker deletion duties, July 1, 2029 for annual statements, July 1, 2031 for audits, July 1, 2027 for streaming volume) (Sec. 1, Sec. 2, Sec. 5, Sec. 6, Sec. 20)
key_definitions: Accessible deletion mechanism: the mechanism established pursuant to subsection (a) of section 5 of this act (Sec. 1(1))
Brokered personal data: one or more specified personal data elements concerning a consumer, if categorized or organized for sale or license to a third party (Sec. 1(3))
Data broker: any business or portion of a business that sells or licenses brokered personal data to another person (Sec. 1(7))
Data service provider: any person who maintains personal data on behalf of a registered data broker (Sec. 1(8))
Deletion request: any request submitted by a consumer under subparagraph (A)(i) of subdivision (1) of subsection (a) of section 5 of this act (Sec. 1(9))
Registered data broker: any data broker that is actively registered as a data broker in accordance with section 2 of this act (Sec. 1(17))
Unregistered data broker: any data broker that is not actively registered as a data broker in accordance with section 2 of this act (Sec. 1(18))

Consumer: has the same meaning as provided in section 42-515 of the general statutes, as amended by this act (Sec. 1(6)); for section 11, an individual who is a resident of this state (Sec. 11(1)); for sections 17-19, any individual physically present in this state and a recipient or prospective recipient of genetic testing (Sec. 17(2)); for section 20, any person physically present in this state and a recipient or prospective recipient of a streaming video service (Sec. 20(3))

Personal data: has the same meaning as provided in section 42-515 of the general statutes, as amended by this act (Sec. 1(16), Sec. 11(6)); defined in section 42-515 as any information that is linked or reasonably linkable to an identified or identifiable individual, excluding de-identified data or publicly available information (Sec. 12(28))

Price setting device: any automated or programmed process that uses a consumer's personal data to establish a price for a consumer good or consumer service to be sold, leased, exchanged or provided to the consumer (Sec. 11(7))

Surveillance pricing: the practice of establishing a customized price for a consumer good or consumer service that is specific to a consumer based, in whole or in part, on the consumer's personal data collected through technology or technological methods and by the person establishing the price directly or indirectly (Sec. 11(9))

Retail seller: a retailer as defined in section 12-407 of the general statutes to the extent engaged in making sales at retail of tangible personal property, including a retail food establishment (Sec. 11(8))

Third-party delivery service: a company, organization or entity outside the operation of a retail food establishment's business that facilitates delivery or online ordering services to customers of a retail food establishment (Sec. 11(10))

Direct-to-consumer genetic testing company: any person doing business in this state who, in the ordinary course of business, offers genetic testing directly to a consumer or collects, uses or analyzes genetic data provided by a consumer, excluding licensed health care providers acting within scope of practice (Sec. 17(4))

Genetic data: any data concerning an individual's genetic characteristics, including raw sequence data, genotypic or phenotypic information, and certain health condition information reported by the individual and analyzed in connection with raw sequence data, excluding de-identified data (Sec. 17(7))

Express consent: an affirmative response by a consumer to a clear, meaningful and prominent notice regarding the collection, use, retention or disclosure of the consumer's genetic data for a specific purpose (Sec. 17(6))
Biological sample: any material derived from the human body and known to contain DNA, including human tissue, blood, urine or saliva (Sec. 17(1))
Streaming video service: any service through which any video content is made available directly to consumers through a distribution method that uses the Internet protocol (Sec. 20(6))
Commercial advertisement: has the same meaning as such term is used in the Commercial Advertisement Loudness Mitigation Act, P.L. 111-311 (Sec. 20(2))

Sensitive data: personal data that includes data revealing racial or ethnic origin, religious beliefs, mental or physical health condition, sex life, sexual orientation, citizenship or immigration status, consumer health data, genetic or biometric data, personal data collected from a known child, victim of crime status, precise geolocation data, neural data, financial account credentials, or government-issued identification numbers (Sec. 12(40))

Precise geolocation data: information derived from technology that directly identifies the specific location of an individual with precision and accuracy within a radius of one thousand seven hundred fifty feet, excluding content of communications or utility metering data (Sec. 12(29))
Dark pattern: a user interface designed or manipulated with the substantial effect of subverting or impairing user autonomy, decision-making or choice (Sec. 12(14))

Consent: a clear affirmative act signifying a consumer's freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous agreement to allow processing of personal data, excluding acceptance of broad terms, hovering, muting, pausing, closing content, or agreement obtained through dark patterns (Sec. 12(7))
Sale of personal data: the exchange of personal data for monetary or other valuable consideration by the controller to a third party, with specified exclusions (Sec. 12(39))

Targeted advertising: displaying advertisements to a consumer where the advertisement is selected based on personal data obtained or inferred from that consumer's activities over time and across nonaffiliated Internet web sites or online applications to predict preferences or interests, with specified exclusions (Sec. 12(41))

Profiling: any form of automated processing performed on personal data to evaluate, analyze or predict personal aspects related to an identified or identifiable individual's economic situation, health, personal preferences, interests, reliability, behavior, location or movements (Sec. 12(32))

Consumer health data: any personal data that a controller uses to identify a consumer's physical or mental health condition, diagnosis or status, including gender-affirming health data and reproductive or sexual health data (Sec. 12(9))
Reproductive or sexual health data: any personal data concerning an effort made by a consumer to seek, or a consumer's receipt of, reproductive or sexual health care (Sec. 12(37))
Facial recognition technology: any technology that analyzes facial features in still images or video to uniquely and personally identify a specific individual (Sec. 12(17))
Neural data: any information that is generated by measuring the activity of an individual's central nervous system (Sec. 12(25))

Biometric data: data generated by automatic measurements of an individual's biological characteristics, such as a fingerprint, voiceprint, eye retinas, irises or other unique biological patterns or characteristics used to identify a specific individual, excluding photographs, audio or video recordings unless generated to identify a specific individual (Sec. 12(4))

De-identified data: data that cannot reasonably be used to infer information about or otherwise be linked to an identified or identifiable individual if the controller takes reasonable measures, publicly commits to de-identified processing, and contractually obligates recipients (Sec. 12(16))

Publicly available information: information made available through federal, state or local government records or to the general public from widely distributed media, or that a controller has a reasonable basis to believe the consumer lawfully made available to the general public, with specified exclusions (Sec. 12(35))
Controller: a person who, alone or jointly with others, determines the purpose and means of processing personal data (Sec. 12(11))
Processor: a person who processes personal data on behalf of a controller (Sec. 12(31))
Third party: a person, such as a public authority, agency or body, other than the consumer, controller or processor or an affiliate of the processor or the controller (Sec. 12(42))

Decision that produces any legal or similarly significant effect: any decision made by the controller that results in the provision or denial of financial or lending service, housing, insurance, education enrollment or opportunity, criminal justice, employment opportunity or health care service (Sec. 12(15))
Minor: any consumer who is younger than eighteen years of age (Sec. 1(13))

License: to grant access to, or distribute, brokered personal data in exchange for consideration, excluding using personal data for the sole benefit of the person who provided it if that person maintains control (Sec. 1(12))

Business: any person who regularly engages in commercial activities for the purpose of generating income, any bank or credit union as defined in section 36a-2, and any person who controls, is controlled by or is under common control with such persons, excluding state bodies or political subdivisions (Sec. 1(4))
Commissioner: the Commissioner of Consumer Protection (Sec. 1(5))
Department: the Department of Consumer Protection (Sec. 1(10))
HIPAA: the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996, 42 USC 1320d et seq., as amended (Sec. 1(11))

Person: has the same meaning as provided in section 42-515 of the general statutes, as amended by this act (Sec. 1(15)); for section 11, any individual, association, corporation, limited liability company, partnership, trust or other legal entity (Sec. 11(5)); for sections 17-19, any individual, association, corporation, limited liability company, partnership, trust or other legal entity (Sec. 17(9)); for section 20, any individual, association, corporation, limited liability company, partnership, trust or other legal entity (Sec. 20(5))
Consumer good: any article that is purchased, leased, exchanged or received primarily for personal, family or household purposes (Sec. 11(2))
Consumer service: any service that is purchased, leased, exchanged or received primarily for personal, family or household purposes (Sec. 11(3))

Discounted price: any price for a consumer good or consumer service that is established for or offered to a consumer or group of consumers and verifiably lower than the generally available, publicly disclosed and bona fide market price (Sec. 11(4))
Abortion: terminating a pregnancy for any purpose other than producing a live birth (Sec. 12(1))
Affiliate: a legal entity that shares common branding with another legal entity or controls, is controlled by or is under common control with another legal entity (Sec. 12(2))
Authenticate: to use reasonable means to determine that a request to exercise consumer rights is being made by or on behalf of the consumer entitled to exercise such rights (Sec. 12(3))
Business associate: has the same meaning as provided in HIPAA (Sec. 12(5))
Child: has the same meaning as provided in COPPA (Sec. 12(6))
COPPA: the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act of 1998, 15 USC 6501 et seq., and regulations, rules, guidance and exemptions adopted pursuant to said act (Sec. 12(12))
Covered entity: has the same meaning as provided in HIPAA (Sec. 12(13))
Gender-affirming health care services: has the same meaning as provided in section 52-571m (Sec. 12(18))
Gender-affirming health data: any personal data concerning an effort made by a consumer to seek, or a consumer's receipt of, gender-affirming health care services (Sec. 12(19))

Geofence: any technology that uses global positioning coordinates, cell tower connectivity, cellular data, radio frequency identification, wireless fidelity technology data or any other form of location detection to establish a virtual boundary (Sec. 12(20))
Identified or identifiable individual: an individual who can be readily identified, directly or indirectly (Sec. 12(22))
Institution of higher education: any individual or entity licensed or accredited to offer one or more programs of higher learning leading to one or more degrees (Sec. 12(23))
Mental health facility: any health care facility in which at least seventy per cent of the health care services provided are mental health services (Sec. 12(24))
Nonprofit organization: any organization exempt from taxation under Section 501(c)(3), 501(c)(4), 501(c)(6) or 501(c)(12) of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986 (Sec. 12(26))
Protected health information: has the same meaning as provided in HIPAA (Sec. 12(33))

Pseudonymous data: personal data that cannot be attributed to a specific individual without the use of additional information, provided such additional information is kept separately and subject to appropriate technical and organizational measures (Sec. 12(34))

Reproductive or sexual health care: any health care-related services or products rendered or provided concerning a consumer's reproductive system or sexual well-being, including abortion-related services (Sec. 12(36))

Reproductive or sexual health facility: any health care facility in which at least seventy per cent of the health care-related services or products rendered or provided are reproductive or sexual health care (Sec. 12(38))
Trade secret: has the same meaning as provided in section 35-51 (Sec. 12(43))
Cable operator: has the same meaning as provided in 47 USC 522 (Sec. 20(1))
Multichannel video programming distributor: has the same meaning as provided in 47 USC 522 (Sec. 20(4))
Television broadcast station: has the same meaning as provided in 47 USC 325 (Sec. 20(7))
Video programming: has the same meaning as provided in 47 USC 613 (Sec. 20(8))
compliance_steps: Determine whether the organisation is a data broker under section 1(7); if selling or licensing brokered personal data in Connecticut, register with the Department of Consumer Protection before January 1, 2027, pay the $2,500 fee, and submit the required application disclosures (Sec. 2(a),(b),(c))
Establish a privacy policy that includes measures to ensure no sale or license of personal data in violation of sections 1 to 10 or sections 42-515 to 42-526 (Sec. 3)

Monitor the accessible deletion mechanism; starting October 1, 2028, access it at least every 45 days, examine deletion requests, delete personal data for verified requests not excluding the broker, direct data service providers to delete, process unverified requests as opt-outs, and repeat every 45 days unless excluded (Sec. 5(c)(1),(2))
If retaining personal data under an exception, ensure it is not maintained, used or disclosed for any other purpose (Sec. 5(c)(5)(B))
By July 1, 2031 and triennially thereafter, retain an independent auditor, maintain audit reports for six years, and submit to the Department upon notice (Sec. 5(d))
If the business was a registered data broker during the preceding calendar year, post the annual statement by July 1, 2029 with deletion request counts (Sec. 6)

If using a price setting device for non-discounted online prices, include the required disclosure in all online advertisements, promotions, labels, statements, displays, images, offers or announcements (Sec. 11(b))
If a retail seller or third-party delivery service, do not engage in surveillance pricing; if offering discounted prices under exceptions, post uniform terms and offer to all consumers (Sec. 11(c))

If a controller under sections 42-515 to 42-526, comply with data minimization, consent for sensitive data, no sale of precise geolocation, no targeted advertising to known minors 13-17, no discrimination, and honor consumer rights including opt-out and correction (Sec. 13, Sec. 14)
If using facial recognition technology on premises for security, use only the organisation's own database and post signage with hyperlink or QR code to the policy (Sec. 16(a)(2))

If a direct-to-consumer genetic testing company, obtain express consents, display privacy notice, implement security measures, provide access, deletion, destruction and revocation processes, and do not disclose to prohibited parties (Sec. 19)
If a streaming video service, ensure commercial advertisement audio is not louder than accompanying video content by July 1, 2027 (Sec. 20(b))
who_it_applies_to: Data brokers (businesses selling or licensing brokered personal data) (Sec. 1, Sec. 2)
Registered data brokers and data service providers (Sec. 5)
Businesses that were registered data brokers during the preceding calendar year (Sec. 6)
Persons doing business in the state who use a price setting device (Sec. 11)
Retail sellers and third-party delivery services doing business in the state (Sec. 11)
Controllers, processors, and consumer health data controllers under sections 42-515 to 42-526, as amended by this act (Sec. 12 through Sec. 16)
notable_exemptions: The provisions of sections 1 to 10 do not apply to consumer reporting agencies, persons furnishing information to consumer reporting agencies, or users of consumer reports to the extent regulated under the Fair Credit Reporting Act (Sec. 7(a)(1))
The provisions of sections 1 to 10 do not apply to financial institutions, affiliates or nonaffiliated third parties to the extent regulated under Title V of the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act (Sec. 7(a)(2))

The provisions of sections 1 to 10 do not apply to a business that collects information concerning a consumer if the consumer is or was in a contractual relationship, an investor, a donor, or a similar relationship with the business (Sec. 7(a)(3))

The provisions of sections 1 to 10 do not apply to a business that performs services for, or acts as an agent of, a business described in subdivision (3) of section 7(a) or a governmental entity (Sec. 7(a)(4))
The provisions of sections 1 to 10 do not apply to a business collecting data used for purposes of the regulation of listed chemicals under 21 USC 830 (Sec. 7(a)(5))
The provisions of sections 1 to 10 do not apply to candidate committees, national committees, party committees or political committees as defined in section 9-601 (Sec. 7(a)(6))
The provisions of sections 1 to 10 do not apply to covered entities or business associates as defined in 45 CFR 160.103 (Sec. 7(a)(7))

An unregistered data broker may sell or license brokered personal data if the sale or licensing exclusively involves publicly available information concerning a consumer's business or profession, health or safety alerts, government records unless collated into a profile or used to generate inferences, digital access to journals or educational works, electronic commerce services or software, directory assistance, or one-time asset dispositions (Sec. 7(b))

The provisions of section 11(b) and (c) do not apply to persons licensed or registered under insurance laws, financial institutions under GLBA, or banks, holding companies, out-of-state banks or out-of-state holding companies supervised by the Banking Commissioner (Sec. 11(d))

The following are not deemed surveillance pricing: offering a discounted price to retain a customer, different prices due to justifiable cost or temporal differences, or discounted prices based on publicly disclosed uniform terms, broadly defined groups, or loyalty programs with affirmative enrollment and posted terms (Sec. 11(c)(2))

A registered data broker or data service provider is not required to delete a participating consumer's personal data and may maintain, use or disclose it to the extent reasonably necessary for specified purposes such as legal compliance, legal claims, providing requested products or services, contracts, safety, security, research, internal operations, and product recalls (Sec. 5(c)(5)(A))

A controller may offer a different price, rate, level, quality or selection of goods or services to a consumer in connection with voluntary participation in a bona fide loyalty, rewards, premium features, discounts or club card program (Sec. 14(a)(2))

Nothing in sections 42-515 to 42-526 restricts a controller's, processor's or consumer health data controller's ability to comply with law, legal claims, provide requested products or services, perform contracts, protect safety, prevent security incidents, engage in public interest research, assist other parties, or process personal data for public health reasons (Sec. 16(a)(1))
Personal data does not include de-identified data or publicly available information (Sec. 12(28))
reading.penalties_and_enforcement: The Commissioner of Consumer Protection, after notice and hearing under chapter 54, may impose a civil penalty of not more than $200 per day for each violation of sections 2 to 8, with penalties deposited in the data broker registration account (Sec. 10). Violations of section 11(b) to (d) (price setting device and surveillance pricing) constitute an unfair or deceptive trade practice under section 42-110b, enforced solely by the Attorney General, with no private right of action and no grounds for an action under section 42-110g (Sec. 11(e)). Violations of section 19(a) (direct-to-consumer genetic testing) are deemed an unfair or deceptive trade practice under section 42-110b, enforced solely by the Attorney General, with no private right of action and no grounds under section 42-110g (Sec. 19(b)). Violations of section 20(b) (streaming video volume) constitute an unfair trade practice under section 42-110b, enforced solely by the Attorney General, with section 42-110g not applying and no private right of action (Sec. 20(c)). For violations of sections 42-515 to 42-526 as amended by this act, the act does not state enforcement or penalties in this text.
how_it_affects_ai_deployment: An organisation using an automated price setting device that increases a price based on personal data must include a specific disclosure in online advertisements, promotions, labels, statements, displays, images, offers or announcements (Sec. 11(b)(1))

Retail sellers and third-party delivery services cannot use surveillance pricing, which is customized pricing based on personal data collected through technology such as biometric monitoring, cameras, device tracking or sensors (Sec. 11(c)(1), Sec. 11(9))

Controllers using profiling for automated decisions that produce legal or similarly significant effects must allow consumers to opt out, question the result, be informed of the reason, review personal data, and correct data for housing decisions (Sec. 13(a)(5)(C), Sec. 13(a)(6))
Controllers cannot process personal data for targeted advertising or sell personal data of known minors aged 13 to 17 (Sec. 14(a)(1)(I))
Controllers and third parties cannot sell precise geolocation data (Sec. 14(a)(3)(A), Sec. 15(a)(2)(A))

Controllers using facial recognition technology on premises for security must use only their own database and post signage with a hyperlink or QR code to the facial recognition technology policy (Sec. 16(a)(2)(A))

Data brokers using automated systems to categorize or organize personal data for sale must register and comply with the accessible deletion mechanism, including deleting personal data upon verified requests (Sec. 2, Sec. 5)

Direct-to-consumer genetic testing companies using AI to analyze genetic data must obtain express consent for collection, use and disclosure, and cannot disclose to employers, insurers, or marketers (Sec. 19(a)(4), Sec. 19(a)(8))

summary: This act requires data brokers selling or licensing brokered personal data in Connecticut to register with the Department of Consumer Protection and participate in a statewide accessible deletion mechanism for consumer deletion requests. It also prohibits certain surveillance pricing and requires disclosure when a price setting device increases a price using personal data, imposes consent and control obligations on direct-to-consumer genetic testing companies, and limits commercial advertisement volume on streaming video services.

What it does

This act requires data brokers selling or licensing brokered personal data in Connecticut to register with the Department of Consumer Protection and participate in a statewide accessible deletion mechanism for consumer deletion requests. It also prohibits certain surveillance pricing and requires disclosure when a price setting device increases a price using personal data, imposes consent and control obligations on direct-to-consumer genetic testing companies, and limits commercial advertisement volume on streaming video services.

Who it applies to

  • Data brokers (businesses selling or licensing brokered personal data) (Sec. 1, Sec. 2)
  • Registered data brokers and data service providers (Sec. 5)
  • Businesses that were registered data brokers during the preceding calendar year (Sec. 6)
  • Persons doing business in the state who use a price setting device (Sec. 11)
  • Retail sellers and third-party delivery services doing business in the state (Sec. 11)
  • Direct-to-consumer genetic testing companies (Sec. 17, Sec. 19)
  • Streaming video services (Sec. 20)
  • Controllers, processors, and consumer health data controllers under sections 42-515 to 42-526, as amended by this act (Sec. 12 through Sec. 16)

Effective date

October 1, 2026 (general effective date; specific compliance dates: January 1, 2027 for data broker registration, July 1, 2028 for accessible deletion mechanism establishment, August 15, 2028 for verification, October 1, 2028 for broker deletion duties, July 1, 2029 for annual statements, July 1, 2031 for audits, July 1, 2027 for streaming volume) (Sec. 1, Sec. 2, Sec. 5, Sec. 6, Sec. 20)

Key definitions

  • Accessible deletion mechanism: the mechanism established pursuant to subsection (a) of section 5 of this act (Sec. 1(1))
  • Brokered personal data: one or more specified personal data elements concerning a consumer, if categorized or organized for sale or license to a third party (Sec. 1(3))
  • Data broker: any business or portion of a business that sells or licenses brokered personal data to another person (Sec. 1(7))
  • Data service provider: any person who maintains personal data on behalf of a registered data broker (Sec. 1(8))
  • Deletion request: any request submitted by a consumer under subparagraph (A)(i) of subdivision (1) of subsection (a) of section 5 of this act (Sec. 1(9))
  • Registered data broker: any data broker that is actively registered as a data broker in accordance with section 2 of this act (Sec. 1(17))
  • Unregistered data broker: any data broker that is not actively registered as a data broker in accordance with section 2 of this act (Sec. 1(18))
  • Consumer: has the same meaning as provided in section 42-515 of the general statutes, as amended by this act (Sec. 1(6)); for section 11, an individual who is a resident of this state (Sec. 11(1)); for sections 17-19, any individual physically present in this state and a recipient or prospective recipient of genetic testing (Sec. 17(2)); for section 20, any person physically present in this state and a recipient or prospective recipient of a streaming video service (Sec. 20(3))
  • Personal data: has the same meaning as provided in section 42-515 of the general statutes, as amended by this act (Sec. 1(16), Sec. 11(6)); defined in section 42-515 as any information that is linked or reasonably linkable to an identified or identifiable individual, excluding de-identified data or publicly available information (Sec. 12(28))
  • Price setting device: any automated or programmed process that uses a consumer's personal data to establish a price for a consumer good or consumer service to be sold, leased, exchanged or provided to the consumer (Sec. 11(7))
  • Surveillance pricing: the practice of establishing a customized price for a consumer good or consumer service that is specific to a consumer based, in whole or in part, on the consumer's personal data collected through technology or technological methods and by the person establishing the price directly or indirectly (Sec. 11(9))
  • Retail seller: a retailer as defined in section 12-407 of the general statutes to the extent engaged in making sales at retail of tangible personal property, including a retail food establishment (Sec. 11(8))
  • Third-party delivery service: a company, organization or entity outside the operation of a retail food establishment's business that facilitates delivery or online ordering services to customers of a retail food establishment (Sec. 11(10))
  • Direct-to-consumer genetic testing company: any person doing business in this state who, in the ordinary course of business, offers genetic testing directly to a consumer or collects, uses or analyzes genetic data provided by a consumer, excluding licensed health care providers acting within scope of practice (Sec. 17(4))
  • Genetic data: any data concerning an individual's genetic characteristics, including raw sequence data, genotypic or phenotypic information, and certain health condition information reported by the individual and analyzed in connection with raw sequence data, excluding de-identified data (Sec. 17(7))
  • Express consent: an affirmative response by a consumer to a clear, meaningful and prominent notice regarding the collection, use, retention or disclosure of the consumer's genetic data for a specific purpose (Sec. 17(6))
  • Biological sample: any material derived from the human body and known to contain DNA, including human tissue, blood, urine or saliva (Sec. 17(1))
  • Streaming video service: any service through which any video content is made available directly to consumers through a distribution method that uses the Internet protocol (Sec. 20(6))
  • Commercial advertisement: has the same meaning as such term is used in the Commercial Advertisement Loudness Mitigation Act, P.L. 111-311 (Sec. 20(2))
  • Sensitive data: personal data that includes data revealing racial or ethnic origin, religious beliefs, mental or physical health condition, sex life, sexual orientation, citizenship or immigration status, consumer health data, genetic or biometric data, personal data collected from a known child, victim of crime status, precise geolocation data, neural data, financial account credentials, or government-issued identification numbers (Sec. 12(40))
  • Precise geolocation data: information derived from technology that directly identifies the specific location of an individual with precision and accuracy within a radius of one thousand seven hundred fifty feet, excluding content of communications or utility metering data (Sec. 12(29))
  • Dark pattern: a user interface designed or manipulated with the substantial effect of subverting or impairing user autonomy, decision-making or choice (Sec. 12(14))
  • Consent: a clear affirmative act signifying a consumer's freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous agreement to allow processing of personal data, excluding acceptance of broad terms, hovering, muting, pausing, closing content, or agreement obtained through dark patterns (Sec. 12(7))
  • Sale of personal data: the exchange of personal data for monetary or other valuable consideration by the controller to a third party, with specified exclusions (Sec. 12(39))
  • Targeted advertising: displaying advertisements to a consumer where the advertisement is selected based on personal data obtained or inferred from that consumer's activities over time and across nonaffiliated Internet web sites or online applications to predict preferences or interests, with specified exclusions (Sec. 12(41))
  • Profiling: any form of automated processing performed on personal data to evaluate, analyze or predict personal aspects related to an identified or identifiable individual's economic situation, health, personal preferences, interests, reliability, behavior, location or movements (Sec. 12(32))
  • Consumer health data: any personal data that a controller uses to identify a consumer's physical or mental health condition, diagnosis or status, including gender-affirming health data and reproductive or sexual health data (Sec. 12(9))
  • Reproductive or sexual health data: any personal data concerning an effort made by a consumer to seek, or a consumer's receipt of, reproductive or sexual health care (Sec. 12(37))
  • Facial recognition technology: any technology that analyzes facial features in still images or video to uniquely and personally identify a specific individual (Sec. 12(17))
  • Neural data: any information that is generated by measuring the activity of an individual's central nervous system (Sec. 12(25))
  • Biometric data: data generated by automatic measurements of an individual's biological characteristics, such as a fingerprint, voiceprint, eye retinas, irises or other unique biological patterns or characteristics used to identify a specific individual, excluding photographs, audio or video recordings unless generated to identify a specific individual (Sec. 12(4))
  • De-identified data: data that cannot reasonably be used to infer information about or otherwise be linked to an identified or identifiable individual if the controller takes reasonable measures, publicly commits to de-identified processing, and contractually obligates recipients (Sec. 12(16))
  • Publicly available information: information made available through federal, state or local government records or to the general public from widely distributed media, or that a controller has a reasonable basis to believe the consumer lawfully made available to the general public, with specified exclusions (Sec. 12(35))
  • Controller: a person who, alone or jointly with others, determines the purpose and means of processing personal data (Sec. 12(11))
  • Processor: a person who processes personal data on behalf of a controller (Sec. 12(31))
  • Third party: a person, such as a public authority, agency or body, other than the consumer, controller or processor or an affiliate of the processor or the controller (Sec. 12(42))
  • Decision that produces any legal or similarly significant effect: any decision made by the controller that results in the provision or denial of financial or lending service, housing, insurance, education enrollment or opportunity, criminal justice, employment opportunity or health care service (Sec. 12(15))
  • Minor: any consumer who is younger than eighteen years of age (Sec. 1(13))
  • License: to grant access to, or distribute, brokered personal data in exchange for consideration, excluding using personal data for the sole benefit of the person who provided it if that person maintains control (Sec. 1(12))
  • Business: any person who regularly engages in commercial activities for the purpose of generating income, any bank or credit union as defined in section 36a-2, and any person who controls, is controlled by or is under common control with such persons, excluding state bodies or political subdivisions (Sec. 1(4))
  • Commissioner: the Commissioner of Consumer Protection (Sec. 1(5))
  • Department: the Department of Consumer Protection (Sec. 1(10))
  • HIPAA: the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996, 42 USC 1320d et seq., as amended (Sec. 1(11))
  • Person: has the same meaning as provided in section 42-515 of the general statutes, as amended by this act (Sec. 1(15)); for section 11, any individual, association, corporation, limited liability company, partnership, trust or other legal entity (Sec. 11(5)); for sections 17-19, any individual, association, corporation, limited liability company, partnership, trust or other legal entity (Sec. 17(9)); for section 20, any individual, association, corporation, limited liability company, partnership, trust or other legal entity (Sec. 20(5))
  • Consumer good: any article that is purchased, leased, exchanged or received primarily for personal, family or household purposes (Sec. 11(2))
  • Consumer service: any service that is purchased, leased, exchanged or received primarily for personal, family or household purposes (Sec. 11(3))
  • Discounted price: any price for a consumer good or consumer service that is established for or offered to a consumer or group of consumers and verifiably lower than the generally available, publicly disclosed and bona fide market price (Sec. 11(4))
  • Abortion: terminating a pregnancy for any purpose other than producing a live birth (Sec. 12(1))
  • Affiliate: a legal entity that shares common branding with another legal entity or controls, is controlled by or is under common control with another legal entity (Sec. 12(2))
  • Authenticate: to use reasonable means to determine that a request to exercise consumer rights is being made by or on behalf of the consumer entitled to exercise such rights (Sec. 12(3))
  • Business associate: has the same meaning as provided in HIPAA (Sec. 12(5))
  • Child: has the same meaning as provided in COPPA (Sec. 12(6))
  • COPPA: the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act of 1998, 15 USC 6501 et seq., and regulations, rules, guidance and exemptions adopted pursuant to said act (Sec. 12(12))
  • Covered entity: has the same meaning as provided in HIPAA (Sec. 12(13))
  • Gender-affirming health care services: has the same meaning as provided in section 52-571m (Sec. 12(18))
  • Gender-affirming health data: any personal data concerning an effort made by a consumer to seek, or a consumer's receipt of, gender-affirming health care services (Sec. 12(19))
  • Geofence: any technology that uses global positioning coordinates, cell tower connectivity, cellular data, radio frequency identification, wireless fidelity technology data or any other form of location detection to establish a virtual boundary (Sec. 12(20))
  • Identified or identifiable individual: an individual who can be readily identified, directly or indirectly (Sec. 12(22))
  • Institution of higher education: any individual or entity licensed or accredited to offer one or more programs of higher learning leading to one or more degrees (Sec. 12(23))
  • Mental health facility: any health care facility in which at least seventy per cent of the health care services provided are mental health services (Sec. 12(24))
  • Nonprofit organization: any organization exempt from taxation under Section 501(c)(3), 501(c)(4), 501(c)(6) or 501(c)(12) of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986 (Sec. 12(26))
  • Protected health information: has the same meaning as provided in HIPAA (Sec. 12(33))
  • Pseudonymous data: personal data that cannot be attributed to a specific individual without the use of additional information, provided such additional information is kept separately and subject to appropriate technical and organizational measures (Sec. 12(34))
  • Reproductive or sexual health care: any health care-related services or products rendered or provided concerning a consumer's reproductive system or sexual well-being, including abortion-related services (Sec. 12(36))
  • Reproductive or sexual health facility: any health care facility in which at least seventy per cent of the health care-related services or products rendered or provided are reproductive or sexual health care (Sec. 12(38))
  • Trade secret: has the same meaning as provided in section 35-51 (Sec. 12(43))
  • Cable operator: has the same meaning as provided in 47 USC 522 (Sec. 20(1))
  • Multichannel video programming distributor: has the same meaning as provided in 47 USC 522 (Sec. 20(4))
  • Television broadcast station: has the same meaning as provided in 47 USC 325 (Sec. 20(7))
  • Video programming: has the same meaning as provided in 47 USC 613 (Sec. 20(8))

Obligations

  • A data broker must not sell or license brokered personal data in this state on or after January 1, 2027, unless actively registered with the Department of Consumer Protection (Sec. 2(a))
  • A data broker that intends to sell or license brokered personal data must submit an application for initial registration with a $2,500 fee, and renew annually with a $2,500 fee (Sec. 2(b))
  • Each registration application must disclose the applicant's name, contact information, primary Internet web site, a publicly accessible web page detailing consumer rights without dark patterns, whether it collects minors' personal data or precise geolocation or reproductive or sexual health data, measures to ensure no unlawful sale, regulatory status, and other required information (Sec. 2(c))
  • Each registered data broker must establish a privacy policy that includes measures to ensure it does not sell or license personal data in violation of sections 1 to 10 or sections 42-515 to 42-526 (Sec. 3)
  • The Commissioner of Consumer Protection must establish and periodically update an Internet web page disclosing registered data broker information and providing access to the accessible deletion mechanism (Sec. 4)
  • The Commissioner must establish an accessible deletion mechanism program by July 1, 2028, with specified features including consumer submission of deletion requests, status checks, updates, broker exclusion, disability accessibility, security safeguards, and consumer explanations (Sec. 5(a)(1))
  • The Commissioner must use a consumer's motor vehicle operator's license number solely to verify deletion requests and updates, and must not share, store or retain it (Sec. 5(a)(2)(A))
  • Each deletion request and update is confidential and not a public record under the Freedom of Information Act (Sec. 5(a)(2)(B))
  • On and after August 15, 2028, the Commissioner or authorized agent must verify deletion requests using the operator's license number and update the mechanism, or specify that unverified requests be processed as an opt-out under section 42-518(a)(5)(B) (Sec. 5(b))
  • On and after October 1, 2028, each registered data broker must access the accessible deletion mechanism at least once every forty-five days to examine deletion requests and updates, and for each verified request not excluding the broker, delete personal data and direct data service providers to delete, or for unverified requests, retain and process as an opt-out (Sec. 5(c)(1))
  • A registered data broker must repeat the deletion actions at least once every forty-five days after first deleting a participating consumer's personal data, unless the consumer submits a verified update specifically excluding the broker (Sec. 5(c)(2))
  • The Commissioner may impose a fee on each registered data broker that accesses the accessible deletion mechanism, not exceeding the cost of providing access (Sec. 5(c)(3))
  • On and after October 1, 2028, a registered data broker or data service provider that deletes a participating consumer's personal data must not maintain, use or disclose any personal data subsequently acquired concerning that consumer (Sec. 5(c)(4))
  • A registered data broker that retains personal data under an exception must not maintain, use or disclose it for any other purpose (Sec. 5(c)(5)(B))
  • By July 1, 2031 and triennially thereafter, each registered data broker must retain an independent auditor to audit compliance with subsection (c) of section 5, prepare an audit report, and maintain the report and materials for at least six years (Sec. 5(d)(1))
  • A registered data broker must submit an audit report and materials to the Department of Consumer Protection within five business days after the department sends notice requiring submission (Sec. 5(d)(2))
  • By July 1, 2029 and annually thereafter, each business that was a registered data broker during the preceding calendar year must post a statement on its primary Internet web site disclosing the total number of deletion requests accessed, how many were responded to by deleting, retaining, or both, and the number retained based on exceptions or exemptions (Sec. 6)
  • A person doing business in the state who uses a price setting device for any reason other than to establish a discounted price in an online transaction and advertises or promotes online a price established by the device must include the disclosure 'THIS PRICE WAS INCREASED BY A PRICE SETTING DEVICE USING YOUR PERSONAL DATA' or a substantially similar disclosure, readily visible to the average consumer (Sec. 11(b))
  • A retail seller or third-party delivery service that offers a discounted price under the exception in section 11(c)(2)(C) must prominently post the discounted price and uniform terms and conditions on its Internet web site in readily understandable language and offer the discounted price to all consumers pursuant to those terms (Sec. 11(c)(2)(C)(I),(II))
  • A controller must limit collection of personal data to what is reasonably necessary and proportionate, not process for new purposes without consent, establish reasonable data security practices, not process sensitive data without consent, not process personal data in violation of discrimination laws, provide an effective consent revocation mechanism, not sell sensitive data without consent, and not process personal data for targeted advertising or sell personal data of known minors aged 13 to 17 (Sec. 14(a)(1))
  • A controller must not discriminate against a consumer for exercising consumer rights (Sec. 14(a)(1) last sentence)
  • A processor must adhere to the instructions of a controller and assist the controller in meeting obligations, including responding to consumer requests, security, breach notification, and data protection assessments (Sec. 15(a)(1))
  • A controller or consumer health data controller that uses facial recognition technology on its premises for security purposes must exclusively use it to match still images or video to a database maintained exclusively by the controller, and post clearly legible signage at each entrance alerting consumers and including a conspicuous hyperlink or quick response code to the facial recognition technology policy (Sec. 16(a)(2)(A))
  • A direct-to-consumer genetic testing company must transact its business consistent with a consumer's rights under section 18 (Sec. 19(a)(1))
  • A direct-to-consumer genetic testing company must disclose its policies and procedures concerning collection, use and disclosure of genetic data prior to accepting any biological sample, genetic data or payment (Sec. 19(a)(2))
  • A direct-to-consumer genetic testing company must display a prominent and publicly accessible privacy notice on its Internet web site disclosing policies and procedures concerning collection, use, access, disclosure, transfer, security, retention and deletion of consumer data and consent (Sec. 19(a)(3))
  • A direct-to-consumer genetic testing company must obtain express consent before collecting, using or disclosing a consumer's genetic data, after disclosing policies, identity of persons who may access results, and manner of disclosure (Sec. 19(a)(4))
  • A direct-to-consumer genetic testing company must separately obtain express consent to disclose or transfer genetic data to any person other than a vendor or service provider, to use genetic data for any purpose other than the primary purpose, or to retain a biological sample after completion of testing (Sec. 19(a)(5))
  • A direct-to-consumer genetic testing company must obtain informed consent in accordance with 45 CFR 46 for any disclosure or transfer of genetic data to a third party for research purposes or research conducted under the company's control for publication or generalizable knowledge (Sec. 19(a)(6))
  • A direct-to-consumer genetic testing company must implement reasonable security measures to protect biological samples and genetic data from unauthorized access, destruction, use, modification or disclosure (Sec. 19(a)(9))
  • A direct-to-consumer genetic testing company must implement a process for a consumer to access genetic data, require deletion of genetic data, require destruction and confirmation of destruction of biological sample, and revoke consent for research use by the company or third parties (Sec. 19(a)(10))

Prohibitions

  • No data broker shall sell or license brokered personal data in this state on or after January 1, 2027, unless actively registered with the Department of Consumer Protection (Sec. 2(a))
  • No data broker shall sell or license any personal data in violation of sections 1 to 10 or sections 42-515 to 42-526 (Sec. 3)
  • No registered data broker or data service provider that deletes a participating consumer's personal data shall maintain, use or disclose any personal data subsequently acquired concerning that consumer (Sec. 5(c)(4))
  • No registered data broker or data service provider that maintains, uses or discloses a participating consumer's personal data for an exception shall maintain, use or disclose it for any other purpose (Sec. 5(c)(5)(B))
  • No person doing business in the state who uses a price setting device for a non-discounted online price shall advertise, promote, label, or publish online a price without including the required disclosure (Sec. 11(b)(1))
  • No retail seller or third-party delivery service doing business in the state shall engage in surveillance pricing (Sec. 11(c)(1))
  • No controller shall sell any consumer's precise geolocation data (Sec. 14(a)(3)(A))
  • No third party shall sell any consumer's precise geolocation data (Sec. 15(a)(2)(A))
  • No controller shall process personal data in violation of any state or federal law that prohibits unlawful discrimination against consumers (Sec. 14(a)(1)(E),(F))
  • No controller shall process sensitive data concerning a consumer without obtaining the consumer's consent, or in the case of a known child, without processing in accordance with COPPA (Sec. 14(a)(1)(D))
  • No controller shall sell the sensitive data of a consumer without the consumer's consent (Sec. 14(a)(1)(H))
  • No controller shall process personal data for targeted advertising or sell personal data of a consumer under circumstances where the controller has actual knowledge or wilfully disregards that the consumer is at least 13 but younger than 18 years of age (Sec. 14(a)(1)(I))
  • No controller shall discriminate against a consumer for exercising consumer rights (Sec. 14(a)(1) last sentence)
  • No direct-to-consumer genetic testing company shall disclose the results of any genetic testing to any person other than the consumer, unless the company has obtained express consent or the disclosure is made pursuant to a court order, warrant or subpoena (Sec. 19(a)(7))
  • No direct-to-consumer genetic testing company shall disclose a consumer's genetic data to the consumer's employer, to any person offering health, life or long-term care insurance or providing information to insurers for underwriting, or to any third party the company knows or reasonably should know intends to use the data for marketing including targeted advertising (Sec. 19(a)(8))
  • No streaming video service shall transmit to a consumer the audio of a commercial advertisement at a volume louder than the volume of the video content that accompanies the commercial advertisement, on and after July 1, 2027 (Sec. 20(b))
  • No controller or consumer health data controller using facial recognition technology on premises for security shall use it other than exclusively to match still images or video to a database maintained exclusively by the controller (Sec. 16(a)(2)(A)(i))

Penalties and enforcement

The Commissioner of Consumer Protection, after notice and hearing under chapter 54, may impose a civil penalty of not more than $200 per day for each violation of sections 2 to 8, with penalties deposited in the data broker registration account (Sec. 10). Violations of section 11(b) to (d) (price setting device and surveillance pricing) constitute an unfair or deceptive trade practice under section 42-110b, enforced solely by the Attorney General, with no private right of action and no grounds for an action under section 42-110g (Sec. 11(e)). Violations of section 19(a) (direct-to-consumer genetic testing) are deemed an unfair or deceptive trade practice under section 42-110b, enforced solely by the Attorney General, with no private right of action and no grounds under section 42-110g (Sec. 19(b)). Violations of section 20(b) (streaming video volume) constitute an unfair trade practice under section 42-110b, enforced solely by the Attorney General, with section 42-110g not applying and no private right of action (Sec. 20(c)). For violations of sections 42-515 to 42-526 as amended by this act, the act does not state enforcement or penalties in this text.

How it affects AI deployment

  • An organisation using an automated price setting device that increases a price based on personal data must include a specific disclosure in online advertisements, promotions, labels, statements, displays, images, offers or announcements (Sec. 11(b)(1))
  • Retail sellers and third-party delivery services cannot use surveillance pricing, which is customized pricing based on personal data collected through technology such as biometric monitoring, cameras, device tracking or sensors (Sec. 11(c)(1), Sec. 11(9))
  • Controllers using profiling for automated decisions that produce legal or similarly significant effects must allow consumers to opt out, question the result, be informed of the reason, review personal data, and correct data for housing decisions (Sec. 13(a)(5)(C), Sec. 13(a)(6))
  • Controllers cannot process personal data for targeted advertising or sell personal data of known minors aged 13 to 17 (Sec. 14(a)(1)(I))
  • Controllers and third parties cannot sell precise geolocation data (Sec. 14(a)(3)(A), Sec. 15(a)(2)(A))
  • Controllers using facial recognition technology on premises for security must use only their own database and post signage with a hyperlink or QR code to the facial recognition technology policy (Sec. 16(a)(2)(A))
  • Data brokers using automated systems to categorize or organize personal data for sale must register and comply with the accessible deletion mechanism, including deleting personal data upon verified requests (Sec. 2, Sec. 5)
  • Direct-to-consumer genetic testing companies using AI to analyze genetic data must obtain express consent for collection, use and disclosure, and cannot disclose to employers, insurers, or marketers (Sec. 19(a)(4), Sec. 19(a)(8))

Notable exemptions

  • The provisions of sections 1 to 10 do not apply to consumer reporting agencies, persons furnishing information to consumer reporting agencies, or users of consumer reports to the extent regulated under the Fair Credit Reporting Act (Sec. 7(a)(1))
  • The provisions of sections 1 to 10 do not apply to financial institutions, affiliates or nonaffiliated third parties to the extent regulated under Title V of the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act (Sec. 7(a)(2))
  • The provisions of sections 1 to 10 do not apply to a business that collects information concerning a consumer if the consumer is or was in a contractual relationship, an investor, a donor, or a similar relationship with the business (Sec. 7(a)(3))
  • The provisions of sections 1 to 10 do not apply to a business that performs services for, or acts as an agent of, a business described in subdivision (3) of section 7(a) or a governmental entity (Sec. 7(a)(4))
  • The provisions of sections 1 to 10 do not apply to a business collecting data used for purposes of the regulation of listed chemicals under 21 USC 830 (Sec. 7(a)(5))
  • The provisions of sections 1 to 10 do not apply to candidate committees, national committees, party committees or political committees as defined in section 9-601 (Sec. 7(a)(6))
  • The provisions of sections 1 to 10 do not apply to covered entities or business associates as defined in 45 CFR 160.103 (Sec. 7(a)(7))
  • An unregistered data broker may sell or license brokered personal data if the sale or licensing exclusively involves publicly available information concerning a consumer's business or profession, health or safety alerts, government records unless collated into a profile or used to generate inferences, digital access to journals or educational works, electronic commerce services or software, directory assistance, or one-time asset dispositions (Sec. 7(b))
  • The provisions of section 11(b) and (c) do not apply to persons licensed or registered under insurance laws, financial institutions under GLBA, or banks, holding companies, out-of-state banks or out-of-state holding companies supervised by the Banking Commissioner (Sec. 11(d))
  • The following are not deemed surveillance pricing: offering a discounted price to retain a customer, different prices due to justifiable cost or temporal differences, or discounted prices based on publicly disclosed uniform terms, broadly defined groups, or loyalty programs with affirmative enrollment and posted terms (Sec. 11(c)(2))
  • A registered data broker or data service provider is not required to delete a participating consumer's personal data and may maintain, use or disclose it to the extent reasonably necessary for specified purposes such as legal compliance, legal claims, providing requested products or services, contracts, safety, security, research, internal operations, and product recalls (Sec. 5(c)(5)(A))
  • A controller may offer a different price, rate, level, quality or selection of goods or services to a consumer in connection with voluntary participation in a bona fide loyalty, rewards, premium features, discounts or club card program (Sec. 14(a)(2))
  • Nothing in sections 42-515 to 42-526 restricts a controller's, processor's or consumer health data controller's ability to comply with law, legal claims, provide requested products or services, perform contracts, protect safety, prevent security incidents, engage in public interest research, assist other parties, or process personal data for public health reasons (Sec. 16(a)(1))
  • Personal data does not include de-identified data or publicly available information (Sec. 12(28))

Compliance steps

  • Determine whether the organisation is a data broker under section 1(7); if selling or licensing brokered personal data in Connecticut, register with the Department of Consumer Protection before January 1, 2027, pay the $2,500 fee, and submit the required application disclosures (Sec. 2(a),(b),(c))
  • Establish a privacy policy that includes measures to ensure no sale or license of personal data in violation of sections 1 to 10 or sections 42-515 to 42-526 (Sec. 3)
  • Monitor the accessible deletion mechanism; starting October 1, 2028, access it at least every 45 days, examine deletion requests, delete personal data for verified requests not excluding the broker, direct data service providers to delete, process unverified requests as opt-outs, and repeat every 45 days unless excluded (Sec. 5(c)(1),(2))
  • If retaining personal data under an exception, ensure it is not maintained, used or disclosed for any other purpose (Sec. 5(c)(5)(B))
  • By July 1, 2031 and triennially thereafter, retain an independent auditor, maintain audit reports for six years, and submit to the Department upon notice (Sec. 5(d))
  • If the business was a registered data broker during the preceding calendar year, post the annual statement by July 1, 2029 with deletion request counts (Sec. 6)
  • If using a price setting device for non-discounted online prices, include the required disclosure in all online advertisements, promotions, labels, statements, displays, images, offers or announcements (Sec. 11(b))
  • If a retail seller or third-party delivery service, do not engage in surveillance pricing; if offering discounted prices under exceptions, post uniform terms and offer to all consumers (Sec. 11(c))
  • If a controller under sections 42-515 to 42-526, comply with data minimization, consent for sensitive data, no sale of precise geolocation, no targeted advertising to known minors 13-17, no discrimination, and honor consumer rights including opt-out and correction (Sec. 13, Sec. 14)
  • If using facial recognition technology on premises for security, use only the organisation's own database and post signage with hyperlink or QR code to the policy (Sec. 16(a)(2))
  • If a direct-to-consumer genetic testing company, obtain express consents, display privacy notice, implement security measures, provide access, deletion, destruction and revocation processes, and do not disclose to prohibited parties (Sec. 19)
  • If a streaming video service, ensure commercial advertisement audio is not louder than accompanying video content by July 1, 2027 (Sec. 20(b))
